entries.name_en: Northern corn leaf blight (Turcicum leaf blight)
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions appear first on the lower leaves.
Lesions are slender, oblong and taper at both ends.
Lesions run along the leaf and may join to cover the whole leaf.
Dusty black-green fuzz appears on the underside where spores form.
Badly hit leaves turn greyish and brittle, like frost-killed leaves.
entries.look_alikes: Gray leaf spot has narrow rectangular tan lesions held between leaf veins. Common rust makes powdery brown pustules, not long cigar-shaped lesions.
cultural_actions: Burn or bury infected maize stubble after harvest.
Scout lower leaves regularly for long tan lesions.
entries.when_to_act: TNAU lists fungicide sprays at two crop growth stages; ask your KVK for current timing and follow product label.

ask_back.question: Are the lesions long, slender and cigar-shaped, tapering at both ends?
Are the lesions narrow rectangles held between the leaf veins?

entries.caveats: TNAU page names Exserohilum turcicum together with another fungus (Helminthosporium maydis); this entry covers the turcicum type. Written for Tamil Nadu. The look-alike line uses a US university-based network page.

symptoms: Tiny flecks appear on both sides of the leaves.
Round to long, cinnamon-brown, powdery pustules break through both leaf surfaces.
Pustules turn brownish black as the crop matures.
In severe cases, the leaf sheaths and other parts are also affected.
entries.look_alikes: Turcicum blight makes long cigar-shaped tan lesions, not powdery pustules.
cultural_actions: Remove alternate host plants near the field.
Collect crop remains and destroy them by burning or burying.
entries.when_to_act: TNAU lists foliar sprays at two crop growth stages; ask your KVK for current timing and follow product label.

ask_back.question: Do you see powdery, cinnamon-brown pustules on both sides of the leaf?
Are the lesions long and cigar-shaped instead of powdery pustules?

sources.title: TNAU Agritech - Common rust of maize

entries.caveats: Written for Tamil Nadu. TNAU page notes cool to warm moist weather favours the disease. Fungicide names are from TNAU only; not checked against CIB&RC.

symptoms: Long, narrow, rectangular, light tan lesions appear on leaves.
Lesions are usually held between the leaf veins.
Lesions may turn gray later.
Symptoms usually start on lower leaves before tasseling.
Heavy leaf damage can weaken stalks and cause lodging.
entries.look_alikes: Turcicum blight lesions are long, cigar-shaped and taper at the ends. Gray leaf spot lesions are rectangular and stay between veins.
cultural_actions: Plant maize varieties or hybrids that tolerate gray leaf spot.
Rotate away from maize; the fungus survives in crop residue.
Use tillage to reduce residue that carries the fungus.
Avoid maize after maize in the same field.

ask_back.question: Are the lesions narrow rectangles, stopped by the leaf veins?
Are the lesions long, cigar-shaped and tapering at the ends?

Burn or bury old maize stubble after harvest.

entries.caveats: No page describing a healthy wheat leaf was found. These lines are the absence of signs listed on cited disease pages. Scouting advice is from the ICAR-IIWBR newsletter.

symptoms: Oval tan-brown lesions, often with a yellow halo, first appear on seedling leaves.
Later lesions follow the leaf veins and have straight edges.
Later lesions usually lack a yellow margin.
In humid weather, a whitish ooze thread may be seen with a hand lens.
entries.look_alikes: Stagonospora blotch and tan spot have more pronounced yellow halos. Septoria lesions are more elongated with rougher edges.
cultural_actions: Choose wheat varieties less susceptible to Septoria.
Let crop residue decompose and rotate crops.

ask_back.question: Are there tan-brown blotches that follow the leaf veins, with little yellow halo?
Are there narrow yellow stripes of powdery pustules instead of blotches?

sources.title: Septoria tritici Blotch of Wheat (Crop Protection Network)
Identification of resistance sources ... Septoria tritici blotch resistance in South Asian bread wheat germplasm (PMC)

entries.caveats: No Indian advisory page was found. The South Asia paper says Septoria is not currently a major concern in South Asia, so confirm the diagnosis with a KVK or university expert. Sources mention labelled fungicides but name no active ingredient, so none is listed.

symptoms: Yellow stripes appear on the wheat leaves.
Stripes are made of pustules holding yellow to orange-yellow spores.
In severe cases it spreads to leaf sheaths, stems and ears.
Leaves dry early and grains may shrivel.
entries.look_alikes: Stripe rust pustules are more yellow than stem rust spores. Leaf rust pustules are scattered, orange to orange-brown; stripe rust forms lines.
cultural_actions: Grow resistant wheat varieties recommended for your area.
Manage nitrogen carefully and avoid excess.
Use crop rotation and mixed cropping as TNAU lists.
Scout fields regularly for early stripes.
entries.when_to_act: Spray promptly when yellow rust is detected, before it becomes an epidemic, as ICAR advises. Report it to your KVK.

ask_back.question: Are the yellow powdery pustules arranged in narrow stripes along the leaf?
Are the spots tan-brown blotches rather than yellow powdery stripes?

symptoms: Small bluish-green flecks grow into spindle-shaped spots with grey centres and brown edges.
Badly hit leaves dry up and wither.
Black lesions on stem nodes can girdle them, and the stem may break.
Grayish-brown lesions on the neck can make the panicle fall over.
Early neck infection can stop grain formation.
entries.look_alikes: Leaf scald has banded tan and brown zones starting at leaf tips or edges, not spindle spots with grey centres.
cultural_actions: Grow resistant varieties listed for your area.
Avoid excess nitrogen; apply it in split portions.
Remove weed hosts.
Burn or bury crop residue after harvest.

entries.cause: Rice stripe virus, spread by planthoppers (virus)
symptoms: Leaves show pale green to yellowish-white stripes.
Leaves may show mottling and dead streaks.
Plants infected young are stunted, with twisted leaves, and may die.
Plants infected later show milder leaf yellowing, with delayed ripening and panicle problems.
entries.look_alikes: Tungro makes leaves yellow or orange-yellow with stunting and is spread by green leafhoppers. Confirm which virus before acting.
cultural_actions: Plant resistant varieties where available.
Time planting to avoid early plant stages during peak insect migration.
Remove crop residue and weeds that keep the virus.
Coordinate planting time with neighbouring farmers.
entries.when_to_act: Sources say to use targeted insecticide against the planthopper vector; the page names no product. Ask your KVK.

ask_back.question: Are leaves yellow or orange-yellow with stunting rather than white stripes?
Are there pale or whitish stripes along the leaves with small planthoppers nearby?

entries.cause: Rice tungro bacilliform virus and rice tungro spherical virus, spread by green leafhopper (virus)
symptoms: Plants are stunted with reduced tillering.
Leaves turn yellow or orange-yellow.
Leaves may show rust-coloured spots.
Flowering is delayed and panicles are small.
Grains are sterile.
entries.look_alikes: Rice stripe virus gives pale or whitish stripes and mottling. Tungro gives overall yellow-orange leaves.
cultural_actions: Plant resistant varieties listed for your area.
Adjust planting dates.
Leave a fallow break between rice crops.
Rotate with pulses or oilseeds.
Plough in stubble and remove weed hosts.

entries.caveats: Written for Tamil Nadu. TNAU lists many insecticides; some are older products. Check current CIB&RC registration and use only the label-recommended one. Insecticides may harm natural enemies.

entries.cause: Leaf-feeding insects such as leaf folder, hispa, thrips and green leafhopper
symptoms: Leaves are folded, or have white scraped patches (leaf folder).
Young seedlings after planting may be damaged badly (hispa, thrips).
Leaves look scorched in severe attacks.
Leaves turn yellow or orange-yellow with stunted plants when leafhoppers spread tungro.
entries.look_alikes: Some disease signs look like insect damage. Leaf scald also looks scorched, and tungro also yellows leaves.
cultural_actions: Find and identify the insect on the plant first, before spraying anything.
Keep field bunds clean.
Limit nitrogen fertiliser.
Ask your KVK or plant protection officer to confirm the pest.
entries.when_to_act: Identify the insect first. For leaf folder, see its own entry, where TNAU gives a damage threshold.
